summary: Gives requirements for Diameter overload control. Existing mechanisms do not handle overload well, so servers can get progressively worse; the document describes the limits and lists requirements for new mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: Diameter is the protocol mobile networks use to ask about subscribers. When the server on the other end is too busy to answer, the RFC asks for a better way to say so: one that says how busy, for how long, and about which part of the service, and that lets the sender back off before the server falls over. The document lists the thirty-four requirements such a mechanism would have to meet.

questions: what to do when a diameter server is overloaded
what does diameter too busy mean
subtitle: What a better way of saying "I am too busy" would have to do for the Diameter protocol.

tldr.problem: When a Diameter server cannot keep up with the requests arriving, it keeps spending effort parsing and answering them, which makes the overload worse. The mechanisms it has today can only say "I am completely unavailable", and only once it already is.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the situations that cause overload, the ways Diameter currently signals a problem, and why they are not enough. It then sets out 34 requirements for a mechanism that lets a node say how loaded it is, for how long, and for which parts of its service.
tldr.outcome: The document is a requirements list, not a protocol. It also sets out what a new mechanism must not do, such as interfere with the transport's own congestion control or make a partially overloaded node harder to use than a healthy one.

today: RFC 7068 is an Informational RFC published in November 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements for a future overload control mechanism and does not define that mechanism itself.

sections.title: What Overload Is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
A Diameter node is said to be overloaded when it has insufficient resources to successfully process all of the Diameter requests that it receives. When a node becomes overloaded, it needs to be able to reduce its load gracefully, typically by advising clients to reduce traffic for some period of time. Otherwise it must keep spending resources parsing and responding to Diameter messages, which can result in a progressively severe overload condition. The existing mechanisms provided by Diameter are not sufficient for managing overload.

The document draws on the work done on SIP overload control and on experience from overload handling in Signalling System No. 7 networks, as well as studies done by the Third Generation Partnership Project. It is worth remembering that Diameter is not usually an end-user protocol. It is generally one component in support of some end-user activity: a SIP server might use Diameter to authenticate and authorise user access, and overload in the Diameter backend will show up to the end user as a worse experience in the SIP application. How that impact reaches the client application is beyond the scope of this document.

Overload here means application-layer overload at a Diameter node. That is different from network congestion, which happens at the lower networking layers. The two are interrelated, and the RFC says network congestion is better handled by the transport protocols: Diameter uses TCP and SCTP, both of which include congestion management features. The document also separates overload from the wider world, since most elements using Diameter applications do not use Diameter exclusively, and an element must be able to tell its Diameter peers that it is overloaded whatever the cause. Signalling overload on protocols other than Diameter is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When a Diameter server cannot keep up, the worst thing it can do is keep answering every request, because answering is what exhausts it. The RFC wants a way to warn senders early, so the load drops before the server goes down.

sections.title: Why Nodes Overload
sections.content:
Overload occurs when an element, such as a Diameter server or agent, does not have enough resources to process all the traffic it is receiving. Resources include the capabilities used to process a request: processor, memory, input and output, and disk. They can also include external resources such as a database or a DNS server, whose own capabilities then form part of the logical element doing the work. External resources can include upstream Diameter nodes, so a Diameter agent can become effectively overloaded if one or more upstream nodes are overloaded.

The RFC lists six kinds of cause. Inadequate capacity: it is very hard to predict every scenario that will raise traffic, and supporting some of them may cost more than an operator thinks worthwhile. Dependency failures: a database, DNS server, disk or network interface fails or becomes overloaded, greatly reducing the logical capacity of the node, so even minimal traffic can tip it into overload. Component failures: a node in a cluster of servers that share the load takes over the work of failed members, and unusual failure conditions can take many nodes down at once, which is often the case with software failures where the same bug hits the whole cluster.

Network-initiated traffic floods are triggered by access network events: operational changes can cause avalanche restarts, frequent radio overlay handovers can generate excessive authorisation requests, and the failure of a Diameter proxy can cause a large amount of signalling as connections and sessions are re-established. Subscriber-initiated traffic floods follow large gatherings or events, such as the finale of a fireworks show followed by many subscribers posting messages, pictures and videos concentrated on one part of a network; smartphone devices with aggressive registration strategies also generate unusually high loads. Finally, a denial-of-service attack can aim a large volume of traffic at one element, from a single source or distributed, so that the volume far exceeds capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Most overload is not a flood of traffic from an attacker. It is a database that got slow, a server that failed, or a crowd of phones all registering at once after a network problem.

sections.title: The Situations the Mechanism Must Survive
sections.content:
The RFC works through the deployment shapes that the mechanism has to cope with. In the simplest peer-to-peer case the client talks straight to the server. If the server becomes overloaded, the client has to reduce the traffic it sends; since it cannot forward requests to another server, it must either queue them until the server recovers or become overloaded itself in the context of its own application.

When the client has several servers for a realm and application, an overloaded Server 1 can be bypassed by sending the traffic to Server 2, provided Server 2 has spare capacity. If Server 1 is approaching overload but can still handle some new requests, it needs to be able to tell the client to move a subset of its traffic rather than all of it. Where the servers host several applications with different resource dependencies, one server can be overloaded for Application A but not Application B, so the server must be able to distinguish between applications in its indication. Where a server is overloaded for all applications, it also needs a way to say so at once rather than notifying the client separately for each application.

Agent scenarios add another layer. With a relay or proxy between client and server, overload can occur at the server, at the agent, or both, but from the client's point of view the two are the same thing. The client usually has no detailed knowledge of the topology beyond the agent, and if the agent uses dynamic discovery the eligible servers may not even be enumerable from the client's perspective, so the agent needs to handle upstream overload in a way that is transparent to the client. A notification about an overloaded upstream server should not be passed back in a way that makes the client think the agent itself is overloaded. There are also cases where the client does need to know about a particular server, such as a request that is part of a multi-round-trip authentication and carries a destination-host attribute naming Server 1.

The interconnect scenario joins two operators' networks, for example over the IP Packet eXchange backbone, which is used to carry Diameter signalling between operators. The information an operator wants to share across that connection is different from what is shared inside its own network, and an operator may not want to convey topology or operational information at all, which limits how much overload information can be sent. The elements in the interconnect network may not support overload control, and the operators may want the information to pass through without further processing even if those elements do support it.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism has to work in several shapes: one server, several servers, a proxy in between, and a link to another operator's network. The hard cases are a server that is overloaded for one service but not another, and a proxy that has to hide an overloaded server behind it without the client blaming the proxy.

sections.title: What Diameter Has Today, and Why It Falls Short
sections.content:
Diameter offers both implicit and explicit ways to learn that a peer is overloaded. The implicit mechanism is simply the lack of responses: if a client does not get a reply in a certain time, it assumes the upstream peer is unavailable or overloaded to the point of effective unavailability. The watchdog mechanism ensures that transaction responses occur at a certain rate even when there is otherwise little or no other Diameter traffic. The explicit mechanisms are protocol error responses, where an agent or server says it is too busy to handle a request with DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY, or unable to route a request to an upstream destination with DIAMETER_UNABLE_TO_DELIVER, perhaps because that destination is itself overloaded. A third is a disconnect peer request message with a disconnect cause of BUSY, which signals the sender's intent to close the transport connection and asks the client not to reconnect.

None of these is enough. The current mechanisms do not let a node shed load as it approaches overload; at best a node can indicate that it needs to entirely stop receiving requests, that is, that it has effectively failed. Even that is problematic, because the transient errors in the base protocol cannot say how long the condition lasts. Diameter offers no way to indicate different overload states for different categories of message, for example a node that is overloaded for one Diameter application but not another.

The implicit mechanism has two specific faults. It cannot tell the client about a problem until it is effectively too late, so the client has no chance to shed load early and avoid collapse. And it cannot distinguish overload of a node from network congestion, because Diameter treats a missing answer as a transport failure. The explicit mechanisms have their own faults. The base specification says a client receiving DIAMETER_TOO_BUSY should send the request to a different peer, and the AAA transport profile recommends failing over all remaining requests, but the base specification does not refer to that profile in its description of the error, so some implementations will keep sending to an upstream peer it has just told to stop. The behaviour also fails the general guidance that an application should avoid sending messages that will never be delivered or processed, since the client tries each request and only discovers the need to fail over when the first attempt fails. There is no guidance on how long to wait before retrying an overloaded destination, and the error can only express overload at the scope of a whole server. Errors and disconnect requests also have no way to say what the scope or cause of the failure was, or how long it lasts.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the only clear signal is silence, and silence means the server has already given up. The one error that does exist says "too busy" without saying how busy, for how long, or about which service, and it is easy for a client to keep talking to that server anyway.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC sets out 34 requirements in seven groups, stated in terms of the behaviour of individual nodes, with the reminder that the overall goal is better system behaviour rather than better behaviour from any one node. The general requirements ask for a way for nodes to exchange load and overload information, for overload control to work whatever applications a node supports, for the impact of overload on the useful throughput of a server to be limited even when the incoming load is far above capacity, for each side of a connection to inform the other of its overload status independently, for the solution to work however peers are discovered, and for the amount of new configuration to be as small as possible, ideally with peers advertising support rather than each node being told about it.

The performance requirements ask for the system to remain stable and for capacity to return to what it would have been once the overload has ended, without oscillations; for nodes to be able to tell current overload information from stale information; for the solution to work across both fully loaded and quiet connections; for consumers to be able to tell when the overload improves or ends; for it to work in networks of different sizes; for a single failing or overloaded node to be limited in its effect on the rest of the network; for no substantial extra work to be imposed on an already overloaded node; for rapid feedback when traffic rises quickly; and for the solution not to interfere with the congestion control of the underlying transport.

The remaining groups cover mixed deployments, where some nodes support the solution and some do not, which must not make things worse and must not let the nodes that do not support it benefit unfairly, and must work between different realms and administrative domains. Any explicit overload indication must be clearly distinguishable from other Diameter errors, and a node that has failed so completely that it cannot signal anything must still get at least the throughput it would have had without the solution. Granular control requires a way to throttle traffic from a peer, graded rather than on and off, enough information for a load balancer to divert throttled traffic elsewhere, and a way to report load levels even before overload happens. Priority and policy requires general guidance on which messages to prefer during overload, while leaving the detailed priorities to the application specification and allowing local prioritisation. The security group forbids new vulnerabilities, forbids assuming that all nodes are trusted, requires a way to restrict what information is sent to which peer, and forbids interfering with existing protection against overload from non-supporting nodes. Finally, the solution must be able to express overload with a granularity of at least the Diameter node, the realm and the Diameter application, must allow further granularities later, must provide a way to extend both the information and the algorithms, must have a default algorithm that every implementation must implement, and should allow information to be exchanged through intermediaries that do not support the solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas run through the thirty-four requirements. A node should be able to say how loaded it is rather than simply whether it is up, and the whole system should keep more useful work done per second while that node is under pressure than it would without any warning at all.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Load and overload information is shared between nodes and directly affects their behaviour, so it is potentially vulnerable to a number of attacks. It may also be sensitive from both a business and a network protection point of view: operators want to control who can see it, so that it cannot be used for competitive intelligence or for targeting attacks.

Sending should be subject to some form of authentication and authorisation of the receiver, and receivers need to be confident that the information they get comes from a legitimate source. The base Diameter specification lacks end-to-end security, which makes it hard for non-adjacent nodes to verify the authenticity and ownership of load and overload information; authenticating it helps.

Four attacks are discussed. A denial-of-service attack is attractive because a small number of messages can cause a large service disruption by falsely reporting overload, and disrupting the overload indications of a server that is already near its limit can stop it mitigating its own condition. A replay attack reuses captured messages at inopportune times, or sends them to other nodes. A man-in-the-middle attack can both read and alter the information exchanged, for intelligence gathering and for direct attacks. The RFC notes that a transport using TLS or IPsec may be desirable for this purpose, and that the base specification's lack of end-to-end security has to be taken into account.
sections.plainLanguage: The load information itself becomes a target. A few forged messages saying "I am overloaded" could bring down a network that trusts them, and operators also treat their load figures as commercially sensitive.

viz.caption: WHAT CAUSES A DIAMETER NODE TO OVERLOAD

items.title: Inadequate capacity
items.text: Traffic scenarios that were never predicted when the network was sized.

items.title: Dependency failures
items.text: A database, DNS server, disk or interface that slows down or fails.

items.title: Component failures
items.text: One server in a cluster fails and the rest take over its load.

items.title: Network-initiated floods
items.text: Avalanche restarts, handovers, or a proxy failure causing sessions to be rebuilt.

items.title: Subscriber-initiated floods
items.text: A crowd of subscribers, or aggressive phone registration, all at once.

items.title: Denial-of-service attacks
items.text: A flood of traffic aimed at one element from one or many sources.

viz.caption: THE EXISTING SIGNALS AND THEIR LIMITS

cells: The client times out and assumes the peer is unavailable
Cannot tell overload from congestion, and arrives too late to act
Keeps responses coming so the link looks alive
Only proves the peer is answering, not how loaded it is
The server says it cannot handle the request
No duration, no scope, and no separate state per application
The server cannot route the request onward
Says nothing about the scope or cause of the failure
The server asks the client not to reconnect
All or nothing, with no indication of how long it lasts

items.title: General (6)
items.text: A way to exchange the information, working for any application.

items.title: Performance (9)
items.text: Stable behaviour, fresh information, and no interference with the transport.

items.title: Mixed deployments (6)
items.text: Works when only some nodes support it, and does not penalise the others.

items.title: Granular control (3)
items.text: Throttling by a peer, diverting throttled traffic, and reporting load early.

items.title: Priority and policy (2)
items.text: Guidance on which messages matter most, and room for local policy.

items.title: Security (4)
items.text: No new weaknesses, no assumption that peers are trusted, and control over who sees what.

items.title: Flexibility (4)
items.text: Granularity down to the node, realm and application, plus room to extend.
